title: Real Women Have Curves
full_review:
A heavyset Latina must decide between college and helping her traditional family in their factory workplace in the well-crafted "Real Women Have Curves" (Newmarket).

At 18, Ana (America Ferrera) is graduating from a good high school in Los Angeles but, unlike her classmates, hasn't applied to college. Her hard-working Mexican-American parents (Lupe Ontiveros and Jorge Cevera Jr.) expect her to now work full time with Mom at her sister Estrela's (Ingrid Oliu) tiny sewing factory, which is in imminent danger of going under.

Ana is depressed at the prospect of working a steam iron all day and further dragged down by her mother's frequent insults about her weight. However, seeing how badly Estrela needs her help, she joins the eight seamstresses, despite the pleas of her teacher (George Lopez) to apply for a scholarship and not waste her mind.

To Ana's surprise, her Anglo classmate Jimmy (Brian Sites) thinks she's lovely and they start secretly dating, with the helpful cooperation of her loving grandpa (Felipe De Alba). Her confidence buoyed, Ana fills out a college application and determines to save her sister from bankruptcy -- and to set her mother straight on beauty being only skin deep.

With music and images, director Patricia Cardoso captures a vibrant East Los Angeles community, centering on one extended and very believable family -- as well as the secondary family that the factory women form. The characters come across as real people with their faults and virtues on display in a script that treats all its characters with compassion, even generosity. Moreover, the film offers a glimpse of the daily toll that poverty takes on individuals who are truly struggling to make ends meet week in, week out.

In her screen debut, Ferrara gives a realistic performance as a conflicted teen, torn between personal and family needs. Ontiveros as well makes her insensitive but loving matriarch a fleshed-out character, clinging to the belief that her daughter should scorn college and focus on getting married and producing children.

George LaVoo's script allows Ana to succinctly express, without undue fuss, the love she has for her family, exasperating as their ideas about a woman's role may be. And through working in a literal sweatshop, Ana comes to appreciate the labor the women around her endure to keep their families going. The scene where she leads them to stripping down to their undies (no men about) to beat the heat is actually heartwarming as well as fun.

Although Ana eventually decides to sleep with her boyfriend, the scene is handled with some discretion, and love, not lust, seems to be the operative emotion. Ana's family is very obviously Catholic, with framed holy pictures and statues throughout the house, but her mother's faith unfortunately comes across more as superstition as she toys with hanging the statue of St. Anthony upside down or removing the infant Jesus from his arms to get a better response to her prayers.

Nor is the lame subplot -- in which Mom insists she is pregnant when it's simply menopause -- as amusing as it intends to be.

All in all, though, "Real Women Have Curves" is a good-looking film with some meat in its message of balancing unselfishness with personal growth and caring.

Some subtitles.

Due to an off-screen sexual encounter and an instance of rough language, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
(
2002
)
